## Power to detect snowmelt trends

With a 10-year record and a residual annual SD of approximately 9 days, the minimum slope detectable by per-pixel regression at the 5% significance level is approximately 2 days/year. The observed mean slope (−0.71 days/year) is far below this detection limit, so a lack of significance is expected regardless of whether a true trend exists. This is why the main text uses trends only to parameterise scenarios, rather than as evidence of change.

## Rationale for excluding trends as predictors: sensitivity analysis adding a trend term to Model B

We added a smooth term for the per-pixel trend, `s(trend)`, to the selected Model B specification and re-evaluated it using the same 4 spatial blocks in leave-one-block-out validation (Table S5).

\setcounter{table}{4}

| Evaluation scope | Baseline AUC | +s(trend) AUC | ΔAUC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Block 1 | 0.9642 | 0.9636 | −0.0006 |
| Block 2 | 0.9091 | 0.9084 | −0.0007 |
| Block 3 | 0.9597 | 0.9595 | −0.0002 |
| Block 4 | 0.9579 | 0.9574 | −0.0005 |
| Pooled | 0.9461 | 0.9456 | −0.0005 |

: Spatial-block validation of the addition of a snowmelt trend term to Model B. AUC decreased consistently in all 4 blocks. {#tbl-s5}

Although `s(trend)` was nominally significant in-sample (edf 3.15, p = 0.011, ΔAIC −8.1), it did not improve prediction in held-out blocks and increased explained deviance by only 0.03 percentage points. Across the central 90% of the trend distribution (−1.84 to +0.12 days/year), the partial effect spanned only 0.13 on the logit scale (odds ratio 1.13), and the 95% band included zero throughout (Figure S4, right). This was negligible compared with the span of the distance term in the same model (5.8 on the logit scale). Thus, the establishment record could not identify a response to trends, and including the trend as a predictor would only add parameters that the data could not constrain.

## Rationale for spatially uniform snowmelt shifts

The scenarios for the 2030 projections apply spatially uniform shifts to snowmelt climatology. We examined the spatial structure of the per-pixel trend field (Figure S4, left). Trends were almost unrelated to elevation (Spearman $\rho$ = +0.022; 50 m elevation bins explained 1.9% of the variance), but showed a **non-monotonic** relationship with snowmelt climatology: means across 10-day bins varied as −0.47 → −1.29 → −0.33 → −0.97 days/year, and the bins explained 24% of the pixel-level variance. Because the relationship was non-monotonic, Spearman $\rho$ was close to zero (−0.007). A uniform shift is therefore an approximation. Nevertheless, the means of all well-sampled bins were negative and within ±0.6 days/year of the landscape mean, with deviations smaller than within-bin variation (SD 0.39–0.77 days/year). The scenario range in the main text (0 / −0.71 / −2.24 days/year) brackets all bin means. Moreover, as shown above, the trend field did not contribute to predicting establishment. A uniform shift is therefore an adequate and deliberately conservative approximation for the purpose of the scenarios.

::: {#fig-s4 layout-ncol=2 fig-pos="H"}
![](files/si/fig_trend_vs_snow_mean.png)

![](files/si/fig_smooth_trend_zoom.png)

Snowmelt trends varied non-monotonically with snowmelt climatology, but their partial effect in Model B was indistinguishable from zero. Left: two-dimensional binned density of per-pixel trends against snowmelt climatology. Red points show bin means ±1 SD. The non-monotonic arch was small relative to the vertical scatter. # Vegetation classification

## Classifier architecture and accuracy

The classifier was a Conv2D–LSTM operating on 5×5-pixel patches, using temporal changes in leaf colour across seasonal image sequences as input. The full installation, image-acquisition, and georectification pipeline followed Okamoto, Ide & Oguma (2024, *Remote Sensing in Ecology and Conservation*).

<!-- Source of every value below: models/crnn.py (architecture, loss, optimiser),
     models/nnmodel.py (folds, checkpointing, per-class report), run_crnn.py
     (epochs, batch size, k, majority vote), utils/utils.py (patch extraction and
     scaling) in the vegetation-classification code base. Class-specific figures
     are fold means from runs/cv/2012_5x5/stratified_cv.csv and
     runs/cv/2021_5x5/stratified_cv.csv. -->

**Input.** Each training or prediction sample was a stack of 7 co-registered seasonal frames covering one 5×5-pixel neighbourhood, i.e. 7 time steps × 3 (RGB) channels × 5 × 5 pixels. Patches were cut from the aligned image series, resampled to the 5×5 kernel, stored as 8-bit values, and rescaled to the interval [0, 1] before entering the network. The two target years were treated as independent series of 7 frames each, and the same network was trained separately on the 2012 and the 2021 series.

**Architecture.** Each frame passed through a single convolutional block — `Conv2d`(3 → 8 channels, 3 × 3 kernel, stride 1, no padding) → PReLU → batch normalisation → `MaxPool2d`(3 × 3, stride 1) — which reduces a 5 × 5 patch to a single spatial position and yields 8 features per frame. The resulting 7-step sequence of 8-dimensional feature vectors was passed to a single-layer, unidirectional LSTM with 7 hidden units (the implementation sets the hidden width to the mean of the convolutional output width and the number of classes, i.e. $\lfloor (8 + 7)/2 \rfloor = 7$). The final hidden state was normalised, passed through one fully connected layer of 7 units with PReLU and batch normalisation, and mapped by a second fully connected layer to the 7 class scores, followed by a softmax. Dropout layers are present but are set to a rate of 0, so the fitted network used none.

**Training.** The loss was cross-entropy and the optimiser RAdam with a fixed learning rate of $1 \times 10^{-3}$; the batch size was 500 and each fold was trained for 50 epochs. No data augmentation was applied: the training and validation transform pipelines are both empty. Training labels comprised 216 hand-drawn polygons, which supplied 618,012 labelled pixels. These were split by stratified 5-fold cross-validation (shuffled, stratified on class), so that each fold trained on 4/5 of the labelled pixels and validated on the remaining 1/5 (mean 123,602 pixels per validation fold). Within each fold the epoch with the lowest validation loss was retained. The published maps are the per-pixel majority vote of the 5 fold models applied to the full image.

Class-specific accuracy is given in Table S12 as the mean across the 5 validation folds. *Sasa*, the focal class, was recovered with an F1 of 0.96 in both years; the weakest class in both years was maple, the rarest of the 7 (12,758 labelled pixels), whose recall fell to 0.90 in 2021. Because the folds were split at the pixel level and the same polygons were reused for both years, these values describe accuracy near the training polygons and are upper bounds on accuracy elsewhere in the scene.

# Spatial verification of *Sasa*→dwarf pine transitions: adjacency analysis

To assess whether *Sasa*→dwarf pine transitions (1,156 cells) were concentrated at the boundaries of existing dwarf pine, we calculated the Euclidean distance from each transition cell to the nearest 2012 dwarf pine cell (Table S6).

\setcounter{table}{5}

| Group | n | $\leq 1.5$ m (directly adjacent) | 1.5–3 m | 3–5 m | >5 m |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| *Sasa*→dwarf pine | 1,156 | **87.5%** | 8.8% | 2.0% | **1.6%** |
| *Sasa*→other vegetation and other classes | 1,312 | 39.6% | 23.6% | 16.9% | 19.9% |
| All 2012 *Sasa* cells (reference) | 8,547 | 46.6% | 27.6% | 15.2% | 10.7% |

: Distribution of distances to 2012 dwarf pine. Of the cells transitioning to dwarf pine, 87.5% were directly adjacent (median distance 1.0 m), approximately 1.9 times the proportion in the reference distribution (46.6%). {#tbl-s6 tbl-colwidths="[32, 11, 21, 12, 12, 12]"}

The transition rate to dwarf pine in the adjacent band ($\leq 1.5$ m) was 25.4%, approximately 6 times that in the 1.5–3 m band (4.3%), and levelled off at around 2% beyond 3 m, consistent with a classification-noise floor. Isolated transitions more than 5 m away amounted to only 19 m² (1.6% of transition area; 10 clusters, maximum 4 m²). Of these, only 2 clusters totalling 5 m², located 21–24 m from the front, were difficult to explain biologically and were consistent with sporadic misclassification within *Sasa* stands.

# Blind interpretation of paired images

We conducted a blind interpretation of paired images to assess whether lateral growth of dwarf pine branches could be distinguished from shifts in the classification of mixed boundary pixels. The 129 samples comprised 79 stratified samples of loss cells (37 to dwarf pine, 30 to other vegetation, and 12 to deciduous shrubs, proportional to the population composition of destination classes, 47/38/15%), 40 stable controls (20 *Sasa* in both years and 20 dwarf pine in both years), and 10 reverse transitions (dwarf pine→*Sasa*). Paired image crops from 2012 and 2021 were presented in random order with transition types concealed. Each sample contained 2 pairs, one from the green-leaf season and one from the autumn-colour season; frames with similar image greenness were paired to reduce phenological differences, and a box marked the projected location of the target 1 m cell. The interpreter (the first author) assigned each sample to one of 4 interpretation categories: *Sasa* loss, canopy cover, boundary ambiguity, or indeterminate. Residual georectification errors could shift the box by 1–2 cells. Boundary ambiguity was used when no clear change was visually discernible.

\setcounter{table}{9}
\begingroup
\small

| Sample group | n | Boundary ambiguity | Canopy cover | *Sasa* loss | Indeterminate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| *Sasa*→dwarf pine | 37 | 73% | **22%** | 3% | 3% |
| *Sasa*→other vegetation | 30 | 87% | 7% | 3% | 3% |
| *Sasa*→3 deciduous shrub classes | 12 | 75% | 8% | 8% | 8%* |
| Stable control (*Sasa*→*Sasa*) | 20 | 85% | 10% | 5% | 0% |
| Stable control (dwarf pine→dwarf pine) | 20 | 80% | **15%** | 5% | 0% |
| Dwarf pine→*Sasa* | 10 | 80% | 10% | 0% | 10% |

: Distribution of blind interpretation judgements by sample group (*percentages may not sum to 100% because of rounding). {#tbl-s10 tbl-colwidths="[34, 6, 17, 13, 11, 19]"}

\endgroup

Judgement distributions were almost identical for loss cells and stable controls. Thus, the interpreter could not distinguish cells mapped as changed from those mapped as unchanged using the photographs. Canopy cover was assigned to 22% (8/37) of *Sasa*→dwarf pine transitions, only slightly above the corresponding judgement for stable dwarf pine controls (15%, 3/20, providing an indication of the false-positive rate). **At the photographic scale, the nature of transitions in individual 1 m cells could not be resolved: whether they represented lateral growth or shifts in classification, or whether *Sasa* survived beneath the canopy.** The main text's interpretation of apparent loss to dwarf pine as a boundary phenomenon therefore rests on the concentration of adjacent transitions (preceding section) and the physical constraint imposed by dwarf pine annual shoot extension (approximately 4–5 cm/year), rather than on this interpretation exercise. We retain the conservative treatment of loss area as an upper bound on true decline. Raw interpretation data and reproduction instructions are included in `review/image_interpretation_package/` in the repository.

![Cells transitioning from *Sasa* to dwarf pine were distributed along the boundaries between persistent *Sasa* and 2021 dwarf pine. This example shows a 300 m window with dense *Sasa*–dwarf pine boundaries. Transition cells are magenta, persistent *Sasa* is dark green, and 2021 dwarf pine is pale green. The window contains 220 transition cells.](files/si/figS7_adjacency_map.png){#fig-s7 width=90% fig-pos="H"}

# Model A

## Table S7: held-out performance and ensemble composition

\setcounter{table}{6}

| Variant | Evaluation scope | AUC | TSS | TSS-maximising threshold |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Main model (full elevation range) | Block mean | 0.949 | 0.785 | — |
| Main model (full elevation range) | Pooled | 0.944 | 0.765 | 0.158 |
| Elevation-restricted (<2,560 m) | Block mean | 0.857 | 0.583 | — |
| Elevation-restricted (<2,560 m) | Pooled | 0.846 | 0.553 | 0.302 |

: Held-out performance of Model A for the full and restricted elevation ranges. {#tbl-s7 tbl-colwidths="[31, 20, 12, 12, 25]"}

The lower performance of the elevation-restricted variant (TSS 0.78→0.58) reflects the ease of discriminating high-elevation cells where *Sasa* cannot occur, rather than deterioration of the model. LASSO stacking retained 4 members in the main model (2 gradient boosted tree models, 1 MaxEnt model, and 1 random forest). Boosted trees and MaxEnt accounted for 95% of the weight, and no GAM members remained.

The full predictor correlation structure is given in Table S11.

Terrain predictors (slope, aspect, TPI, and TWI) were computed from the Fundamental Geospatial Data DEM of the Geospatial Information Authority of Japan (approximately 5 m mesh) [@GSIdem] in QGIS using SAGA GIS tools, and then reprojected to the 1 m analysis grid by bilinear interpolation. The effective resolution of the terrain predictors is therefore that of the source DEM rather than 1 m.

# Model B

## Selection of the distance-term specification

We selected the distance-term specification by comparing a smooth on the linear distance axis, `s(d)`, with a smooth on log-transformed distance, `s(log(1+d))`, using 3 criteria fixed in advance (Table S8).

\setcounter{table}{7}

| Criterion | Requirement | Result | Decision |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Deterioration in pooled AUC | $\leq 0.005$ | −0.0096 (improvement) | Pass |
| Reduction in absolute error in the 0–5 m band | $\geq 30\%$ | 87.3% reduction | Pass |
| Deterioration in the 5–20 m band | None | Improvement | Pass |

: Comparison of distance-term specifications using predefined criteria (linear axis → log distance). All 3 criteria were met, so `s(log(1+d))` was selected. {#tbl-s8 tbl-colwidths="[38, 18, 29, 15]"}

The selected specification achieved block-specific AUC of 0.91–0.96 (pooled AUC 0.946, TSS 0.75). The gradient boosted tree ensemble used as a robustness comparison, fitted to the same response, predictors, and folds, achieved a pooled AUC of 0.948, indicating that the additive model captured nearly all the signal available to a flexible learner. MaxEnt was excluded from the comparison because quasi-separation of the classes along the distance gradient prevented convergence of the regularisation path in `maxnet`/`glmnet`. <!-- TODO: Add a table of sensitivity to smooth basis dimension (k sensitivity); run the analysis and transcribe the results when preparing the English SI. -->

# Cellular-automaton projections

## Exactness of the decomposition and random-number control

The environmental component of the linear predictor was precomputed for each scenario × year, and only the distance term was updated within the simulation. The maximum reconstruction error of this decomposition was $|\Delta p_9| < 8.3\times10^{-11}$ (checked on 10,000 cells; tolerance $1\times10^{-6}$), so the decomposition can be regarded as exact. Each replicate was assigned a fixed random seed, independently of parallel scheduling.

## Validation and structural sensitivity

The hindcast initialised from the 2012 distribution reproduced observed gross expansion with a ratio of 1.077 (expected 4,414 m² vs observed 4,093 m²), and cell-level AUC was 0.92. In spatial-block-exclusion validation, AUC ranged from 0.79 to 0.86 and block-level ratios of expected to observed area ranged from 0.67 to 2.0. Structural sensitivity is summarised in Table S9.

\setcounter{table}{8}

| Sensitivity setting | Expected area in 2030 (s = −0.71) | Ratio to baseline |
|---|---:|---:|
| Baseline | 5,730 m² | 1.00 |
| Remove the 5 m² patch rule | 17,226 m² | 3.01 |
| Replace annualisation with the first-order approximation $p_9/9$ | 5,326 m² | 0.93 |

: Structural sensitivity of projected establishment area. {#tbl-s9 tbl-colwidths="[45, 35, 20]"}

## Table S3: projection summary by scenario

\setcounter{table}{2}

| Scenario | Expected new establishment area by 2030 | SD across replicates | Number of replicates |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| s = 0 (no change) | 4,901 m² | 70 | 200 |
| s = −0.71 days/year (point estimate) | 5,730 m² | 84 | 200 |

The extreme scenario (−2.24 days/year) yielded less establishment than the point-estimate scenario. At sites immediately adjacent to the front, where establishment was concentrated, excessive snowmelt advance shifted conditions beyond the favourable snowmelt window (Section 4.2 of the main text).

The allocation to the *Vaccinium vitis-idaea*–*Pinus pumila* community reflects the scale mismatch between 1:25,000 polygons and the 1 m grid (herbaceous cells within the polygons), rather than establishment beneath dwarf pine canopies.
